header.name: Non-Classical Logics
header.description: This course aims to draw attention to logical systems that are different from classical or standard mathematical logic. Classical logic has been very successful in various ways, not the least of which is in being able to provide a firm foundation for mathematics. Despite this, many of the interesting developments in logic in the past few decades, especially in philosophy and computer science, have occurred in areas such as intuitionism, paraconsistent logics, modal and temporal logics, quantum logic, fuzzy logic, and so on. These are all logics which are intended either to supplement classical logic, or else to replace it where it doesn’t fit. Such logics are grouped together under the umbrella term ‘non-classical logics’. In this course, we will cover some of these systems restricting ourselves only to the propositional cases. We will also give an introduction to analytic tableaus, which have gained popularity as a decision procedure among logicians and computer scientists. The subject could be of interest to students in both Mathematics and Computer Science. The topics covered will include a very brief review of classical propositional logic, semantic tableaus, basic modal logic, intuitionistic logic, paraconsistent and many-valued logics.
prerequisites_mandatory: Knowledge of basic set theory, including definitions and basic properties of union, intersection, complementation, power sets, relations, and functions.

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Students will be able to appreciate the differences between classical and non-classical logics and also the differences between the various non-classical systems.

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Students will be able to construct semantic tableaus to check if a formula of a given logic is valid/ invalid; if a set of formulas of a given logic is satisfiable or not; if a formula is a consequence of a set of formulas in a given logic.

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Students will be able to construct a model for a formula (set of formulas) in a given logic if it is satisfiable.

resources.title: An Introduction to Non-classical logics by Graham Priest
Introduction to Mathematical Logic by Elliot Mendelson
Logic and Structure by Dirk van Dalen
Logic in Action by Johan van Benthem, Hans van Ditmarsch, Jan van Eijck, Jan Jaspars
